  • Charles G. Finney, Lectures to Professing Christians, especially “Love Is the Whole of Religion”
  • Ochorus Originals, Open Your Mouth Wide, especially “Four Young Men at Kells”

fields.title: The Family Altar
fields.body_html:
“Keep these words that I am commanding you today close to your heart. Teach them carefully to your children, and speak of them as you sit in your house and as you go on your way, as you lie down and as you rise.” (Deuteronomy 6:6-7)

In Volume 9 (chapter 15) we visited a narrow old house in Haarlem, in the Netherlands. The family lived upstairs, above a small watch shop, and they called their home “the Beje.” Casper ten Boom was the watchmaker. His daughter Corrie, the youngest of his children, became the first woman in the Netherlands licensed as a watchmaker.

Picture the table after breakfast. Around it sit Casper and his family, the workers from the shop, and whoever else is staying, for the house is always full of guests, foster children and people in need. Casper opens the Bible and reads aloud. Then he prays. In the evening, when the shop is closed, they gather again, and he reads and prays once more. It is not a long service. It is simply what the family does, every morning and every evening, year after year.

Then came the war. When the German army occupied the Netherlands, the ten Booms hid Jews and others in danger in their home. In February 1944 the house was raided and the family was arrested. Casper, eighty-four years old, died in prison about ten days later. Corrie and her sister Betsie were sent at last to Ravensbrück, a terrible concentration camp in Germany.

They had lost their home, their father and their freedom, but not the habit of that table. Corrie had smuggled in a small Bible. As she tells it in The Hiding Place, written many years later, the sisters began to hold Bible readings in their crowded, flea-filled barracks, every day and sometimes twice. Women from many nations gathered round. Corrie read aloud, others passed the words on in their own languages, and Betsie prayed.

The family altar had been carried out of Haarlem, through prisons and camps, into one of the darkest places on earth. What a father did faithfully at his table became a light for many women who had never sat at it.

Prayer at home through the ages

Hannah poured out her soul to God for a child, and when Samuel was born she gave him back to the LORD (Volume 1, chapter 5). Centuries later, Paul remembered the “sincere faith” of young Timothy, “which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). The grandmother taught the mother, and the mother taught the son (Volume 3, chapter 18). The Roman officer Cornelius “feared God, as did his whole household,” and “prayed to God at all times” (Acts 10:2).

In the fourth century, Macrina turned her family’s country house in Pontus into a home of prayer. From girlhood, her brother wrote, the Psalms went with her through every part of her day (Volume 4, chapter 12). In North Africa, Monica lived with a husband who did not believe and had a hot temper. She prayed for him, and for her wandering son Augustine, for years, and before he died her husband came to Christ (Volume 4, chapter 15).

In the 1640s and 1650s, Richard Baxter gave a small book to every family in Kidderminster, and a Bible to the poor families who had none. In time, he wrote, on Sundays you could hear families singing psalms as you walked through the streets (Volume 6, chapter 14). In Japan, where Christians had to hide for more than two hundred years, parents taught the prayers to their children by mouth, softly, so the neighbors would not hear (Volume 6, chapter 10). In a crowded rectory in England, Susanna Wesley gave each child one evening a week alone with her to talk about their souls (Volume 7, chapter 6). And in our own day the short songs of Taizé, each a single line of Scripture or prayer, are easy to carry home and simple enough for anyone to learn, children included (Volume 10, chapter 4).

At home, on the road, at night and in the morning

When Moses spoke the words of our verse, Israel was about to enter a new land. He had just given them the great command: “Hear, Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. You are to love the LORD your God with your whole heart, with your whole being, and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:4-5). Jesus called this the first of all the commandments (Mark 12:29-30). Jewish families have said these words morning and evening for many centuries.

Notice the order of the verses. First, “keep these words ... close to your heart.” Only then, “teach them carefully to your children.” We cannot pass on what we do not hold. Children learn more from what they see in us than from what we say.

Then notice the four times Moses names: sitting at home, walking on the road, lying down and getting up. These are the ordinary moments of every day. Prayer in the home is not mainly a long meeting. It is God’s word woven into meals, journeys, bedtimes and mornings.

George Whitefield, preaching on family religion in the 1700s, gave a simple reason why a household should pray together, and not only one by one:

“Besides, there are no families but what have some common blessings, of which they have been all partakers, to give thanks for; some common crosses and afflictions, which they are to pray against; some common sins, which they are all to lament and bewail: but how this can be done, without joining together in one common act of humiliation, supplication, and thanksgiving, is difficult to devise.”

George Whitefield, Selected Sermons of George Whitefield

A “cross” here means a shared trouble. Every home has blessings, troubles and sins that belong to all who live in it. So every home has something to pray about together.

What is learned at home also lasts. Charles Spurgeon noticed it among the old men of his church:

“At any rate, I have shaken hands with greyheaded men who have forgotten nearly all the events which have intervened between their old age and the time of their childhood, but little matters which transpired at home, hymns learned at their mother’s knee, and words spoken by their father or sister, have lingered with them. The voices of childhood echo throughout life. The first learned is generally the last forgotten.”

Charles H. Spurgeon, Come Ye Children

Three key insights

  1. God’s words must live in our own hearts before we can pass them on at home. Moses put the heart before the teaching. A parent, grandparent or older friend who loves God’s word will pass it on, often without knowing it.
  2. Prayer at home is woven into ordinary moments: at the table, on the road, at bedtime and on waking. Deuteronomy names the plain times of every day. A few words of Scripture and prayer at those times can shape a whole household.
  3. Every believer has a household to pray for, whether married or single, with children or without. Macrina, Amy Carmichael and the ten Boom sisters never married, yet each became the heart of a praying family. God “gives the lonely a home to live in” (Psalm 68:6).

For us today

Homes are very different: three generations in two rooms in Manila or Nairobi, a widow alone in a flat in Seoul, a home where only one person follows Jesus, parents who work long hours or cannot read at all.

The witnesses speak to each of these homes. If you live alone, remember that Amy Carmichael never married, yet at Dohnavur in India the rescued children called her Amma, “mother” (Volume 9, chapter 8). Your household may be the neighbors, friends and church family God has given you. If you long for children and have none, Hannah’s tears were heard, and so are yours. If your husband or wife does not believe, take heart from Monica, and from Peter’s promise that “your way of life will win them over even without your saying a word” (1 Peter 3:1). If your home is crowded, remember Susanna’s apron. If you cannot read, remember the hidden Christians of Japan, who passed on their prayers by heart for about two hundred and fifty years.

No home is too poor, too busy or too broken to become a place of prayer.

Try this

This week, make your home a place of prayer, in small and simple ways.

  • Pray at one meal. Before one meal each day, give thanks together and say one verse aloud. Let a child choose the verse.
  • Use the four times. Choose one short verse, such as Deuteronomy 6:5, and say it as you sit at home, as you go out, as you lie down and as you rise.
  • Ask two questions at night. Before sleep, ask your household, “What can we thank God for today? What shall we ask Him for?” Then pray in a few words. If you live alone, ask yourself, and pray for a friend by name.
  • Sing one line. Learn a one-line song of prayer, such as “Jesus, remember me when You come in Your kingdom” (Luke 23:42), and sing it together until even the youngest knows it by heart.

A closing prayer

Lord our God, You are one, and I want to love You with all my heart, my soul and my strength. Thank You for Hannah, Lois and Eunice, Macrina and Monica, Susanna Wesley and the ten Boom family, and for every parent and grandparent who made a home into a place of prayer. Keep Your words close to my heart, so that I may speak of them at home and on the road, when I lie down and when I rise. Bless my household, whoever is in it. Give the lonely a home, give the childless a family in Your church, and win to Yourself those in our homes who do not yet believe. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Who first taught you to pray? What do you remember of their words or their example?
  • Which of the four times in Deuteronomy 6:7, sitting at home, walking, lying down or getting up, could you most easily fill with a word of prayer?
  • Who belongs to your “household” of prayer, and how could you pray with them or for them this week?

Read more on Ochorus

  • George Whitefield, Selected Sermons of George Whitefield, especially “The Great Duty of Family Religion”
  • Charles H. Spurgeon, Come Ye Children, especially “As a Little Child”
  • Ochorus Originals, The Fire on the Altar, especially “The Apron over Her Head”

fields.title: A Rule of Prayer
fields.body_html:
“It is a good thing to thank the LORD, to sing and play in praise of Your name, Most High, to tell of Your loyal love at sunrise and of Your faithfulness through the nights...” (Psalm 92:1-2)

In Volume 1 (chapter 14) we met Daniel in Babylon as an old man. He had been carried there as a captive in his youth, and he had never gone home. For more than sixty years he had served foreign kings. Now he was one of the highest officials in the Persian kingdom.

Jealous men found a way to trap him. They persuaded King Darius to sign a law: for thirty days, anyone who prayed to any god or person except the king would be thrown to the lions. They knew Daniel would not obey it.

Look at what Daniel did when he heard the news. He did not call a meeting or write a protest. He did not hide. He climbed the stairs to the upper room of his house, where the windows opened toward Jerusalem, far away across the desert. There he knelt down. “Three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had always done” (Daniel 6:10).

The most important words are the last ones: just as he had always done. Daniel had no new plan for the day of danger. He had an old habit. Morning, noon and evening, for year after year, in a city full of idols, he had stopped his work, turned his face toward the city of God’s promise and given thanks. The habit had been built on ordinary days, when no one was watching and nothing was at stake. When the hard day came, the habit was already there to hold him.

The Bible tells us that God shut the lions’ mouths. But the story does not begin in the lions’ den. It begins at an open window, three times a day, for a lifetime.

A rhythm through the centuries

Christians have often called such a pattern a rule of prayer. In this sense a rule is not a law that condemns us. It is more like a measuring line, or the frame that holds up a young vine: something simple that helps our prayer grow straight. The cloud of witnesses has much to teach us here.

Three times a day. David prayed “at evening, at morning and at noon” (Psalm 55:17). Peter and John went up to the temple “for the afternoon prayer at three o’clock” (Acts 3:1; Volume 3, chapter 3). Around AD 100 the Didache, a handbook for new believers, wrote out the Lord’s Prayer and then said, in an old English translation, “Thrice in the day thus pray” (Volume 4, chapter 1). Brother Roger of Taizé kept prayer three times a day, alone at first and later with his brothers (Volume 10, chapter 4).

The whole day turned to God. Benedict built his monks’ day around seven times of prayer, from Psalm 119:164, yet he called his Rule a little rule for beginners (Volume 5, chapter 1). Columba of Iona blessed a pail of new milk, a knife, a barn and an old work horse, and Celtic believers learned to bring ordinary tasks to God in short blessings (Volume 5, chapter 4). The Russian pilgrim learned to carry the Jesus Prayer, “Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me,” into every hour (Volume 8, chapter 6).

Morning and evening. Luther told his barber to make prayer the first business of the morning and the last of the night, and warned him that if we put prayer off until this job or that one is finished, the hour never comes (Volume 6, chapter 2). Ignatius of Loyola taught a short look back over each day, beginning with thanks (Volume 6, chapter 8). In Korea, Kil Sun-ju opened the dawn to the whole church, and Korean churches around the world still meet to pray before sunrise (Volume 9, chapter 5).

A plan to share. Robert Murray M’Cheyne gave his church in Dundee a calendar for reading the Bible, so that they could feed “in the same portion of the green pasture at the same time” (Volume 8, chapter 4). Yet he warned them, “Let the calendar perish rather than this rust eat up your souls.” The plan was there to serve their thirst for God, not to replace it.

Love at sunrise, faithfulness at night

The heading of Psalm 92 calls it a song for the Sabbath day. It begins by saying that praise is “a good thing,” and then it gives each end of the day its own song. In the morning we tell of God’s “loyal love.” In the night we tell of His “faithfulness.”

Think about why. In the morning, the day lies ahead of us, and we need to remember that His love goes before us into it. At night, the day lies behind us, and we look back and see that He was faithful in it, even when we were not. Every day begins and ends in God.

Andrew Murray, who wrote much about the morning hour of prayer, warned that the time alone with God is not the goal in itself:

“The morning watch must not be regarded as an end in itself. It is not sufficient that it gives us a blessed time for prayer and Bible study, and so brings us a certain measure of refreshment and help. It is to serve as a means to an end. And that end is to secure the presence of Christ for the whole day.”

Andrew Murray, The Inner Chamber

That is the purpose of any rule of prayer. Morning, midday and evening are like stones laid across a stream. They are not the destination. They help us walk with Christ through the whole day.

When we fail

Every honest believer who has tried to keep a rule of prayer has failed to keep it. We oversleep. A child is sick. Work runs late. Days, even weeks, slip by. Then we are tempted to give up, or to punish ourselves with guilt.

Francis de Sales, whom we met in Volume 6 (chapter 9), wrote for busy people who kept falling short. In a chapter on being gentle with ourselves, he imagined how we might speak to our own heart after a fall:

“Poor heart! so soon fallen again into the snare! Well now, rise up again bravely and fall no more. Seek God’s Mercy, hope in Him, ask Him to keep you from falling again, and begin to tread the pathway of humility afresh.”

Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life

God’s mercies, Jeremiah said, “are new each morning” (Lamentations 3:23). So is the chance to begin again.

Three key insights

  1. A rule of prayer is a help for weak people, not a prize for strong ones. Benedict called his rule a little rule for beginners. A simple pattern carries us on the days when feeling and strength fail.
  2. Morning and evening each have their own song: God’s love at sunrise and His faithfulness through the night. Psalm 92 teaches us to greet the day by trusting His love and to close it by thanking Him for His faithfulness.
  3. When we fail to keep our rhythm, we begin again gently, because God’s mercy is new every morning. A missed hour is not the end of a life of prayer. The way back is not anger at ourselves but a quiet return to God.

For us today

Your rule of prayer will not look like a monk’s, or like your pastor’s. A mother with a baby, a farmer who rises before dawn, a factory worker on night shifts, a student in a shared room and a prisoner in a cell will each pray at different times. That is good. The witnesses kept many different patterns. What they shared was faithfulness, not sameness.

Begin small. Five minutes kept every day is better than an hour kept once a month. Choose times that already exist in your day: waking, a meal, the walk to work, the moment the lights go out. If you can, share part of your rhythm with others: a family at the table, friends who agree to pray at noon, a church that meets before dawn. And if you have no Bible of your own, you can still keep a rule with the words you know by heart.

Try this

This week, write down a simple rule of prayer, small enough to keep. Here is one pattern to begin with.

  • Morning: love. Before you look at your phone or begin your work, thank God for His loyal love, and pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly.
  • Midday: a short cry. At noon or at your midday meal, stop for one breath and pray, “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me,” or another short prayer you love.
  • Evening: faithfulness. Before sleep, look back over the day with God. Thank Him for one thing, tell Him one thing you regret, and give Him tomorrow.
  • Once a week: together. Choose one time each week to pray with at least one other person, in person or by phone.

A closing prayer

Most High God, it is a good thing to thank You, to tell of Your loyal love in the morning and of Your faithfulness through the night. Thank You for Daniel at his open window, for the first believers who prayed three times a day, for Benedict and the monks of every land, for Luther, Ignatius, Kil Sun-ju and M’Cheyne, and for all who have shaped their days around You. Help me to make a small rule and to keep it. When I fail, do not let me give up or hide from You. Lift up my heart, forgive me, and let me begin again, so that my whole day belongs to You, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

Questions for reflection

  • Daniel prayed “just as he had always done.” What habits of prayer, if any, already shape your days?
  • Which times in your day could become times of prayer: waking, meals, travel, work breaks or bedtime?
  • How do you usually respond when you fail to pray as you planned? What would it look like to begin again gently?

Read more on Ochorus

  • Andrew Murray, The Inner Chamber, especially “The Morning Hour”
  • Francis de Sales, Introduction to the Devout Life, especially “On Gentleness towards Ourselves”
  • Ochorus Originals, Faithful unto Death, especially “Three Times a Day”

fields.title: “Come, Lord Jesus”
fields.body_html:
“The One who testifies to all this says, ‘Yes, I am coming soon!’ Amen! Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20)

In the autumn of 1747, in the house of Jonathan Edwards at Northampton, Massachusetts, a young man lay dying. In Volume 7 (chapter 10) we followed David Brainerd through the snowy forests of New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, praying for the Native peoples he had come to serve. Now he was twenty-nine years old, and tuberculosis had worn his body out. Edwards’s daughter Jerusha, a girl of seventeen, nursed him day after day.

He was waiting for his brother John to come from New Jersey, and John was late. He could no longer work. Yet his mind was clear, and he still prayed for the people he loved. On 2 October he wrote in his diary for the last time:

“I felt sweetly disposed to commit all to him, even my dearest friends, my dearest flock, my absent brother, and all my concerns for time and eternity. O that his kingdom might come in the world; that they might all love and glorify him for what he is in himself; and that the blessed Redeemer might ‘see of the travail of his soul, and be satisfied!’ O come, Lord Jesus, come quickly! Amen.”

David Brainerd, The Life and Diary of David Brainerd

Edwards, who later published the diary, added a note: here it ends. These were the last words written in it.

Two days later, someone came into the room with a Bible in her hand. Brainerd spoke of that “dear book,” and said, “I shall soon see it opened!” On 9 October 1747 he died.

Notice what his last prayer held together. He longed to be with Christ. But he did not forget the world. In the same breath he prayed for his friends, for his little church among the Native people, and for God’s kingdom to come over all the earth. Then he ended where the whole Bible ends: “Come, Lord Jesus.”

Golden bowls

This series takes its name from a vision. In Volume 3 (chapter 20) we stood with the apostle John, an old prisoner on the island of Patmos, as heaven’s door opened before him. He saw the Lamb who had been slaughtered, and around Him the elders bowing low. “Every one of them had a harp, and they held gold bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of God’s holy people” (Revelation 5:8). Later he saw an angel at the golden altar, and “the smoke of the incense rose with the prayers of God’s holy people from the angel’s hand before God” (Revelation 8:4).

Think of a bowl. A bowl is made to hold things and keep them. It is filled little by little. And when John looked, the bowls were already full.

Whose prayers were in them? Through these eleven volumes we have tried to find out. Abraham’s pleading for Sodom. Hannah’s silent tears at Shiloh. Daniel’s thanks at his open window. The prayers of Jesus on the mountain at night. Polycarp’s long prayer before he died. Monica’s tears for her son. The whispered prayers of Japan’s hidden Christians, the Moravians’ watch, the dawn prayers of Korea, the songs of a woman in a shipping container in Eritrea. And millions of prayers no book records: a grandmother’s in a village in Ghana, a prisoner’s in a cell, a child’s at bedtime.

Not one of them was spilled. Many of these believers died without seeing all they asked for. Their prayers wait in the same bowls as ours, and on the day Christ comes, God will answer them in full.

The church’s last prayer

That is why the church has always ended its prayers by looking for Him. Paul closed his first letter to Corinth with words in Aramaic, the language of the first believers: Marana tha, “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22). The Didache, which we met in Volume 4 (chapter 1), gave the church a prayer of thanks after the Lord’s Supper. It asks God to gather His church “from the four winds” into His kingdom, and then it cries, in an old English translation, “Let grace come, and let this world pass away,” and ends, “Maran atha. Amen.”

Others waited with the same longing. Old Simeon and the widow Anna waited in the temple for the first coming of Jesus (Volume 1, Conclusion). The martyrs under the altar cried, “How long?” (Revelation 6:10). In Korea, during long years of foreign rule, Kil Sun-ju preached more and more about the return of Christ, the final dawn when every wrong will be put right (Volume 9, chapter 5).

To pray “Come, Lord Jesus” is not to run away from the world. Jesus said that the gospel “will be announced throughout the world, so that every nation hears the witness, and only then will the end come” (Matthew 24:14). Peter wrote that the Lord is patient, because He “wants all people to turn back in repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). So the prayer for His coming always carries a second prayer inside it, as it did for Brainerd: “O that his kingdom might come in the world.” Those who long for the King pray and work for His people while they wait.

Waiting is not easy. Charles Spurgeon knew how weary believers grow, and how the promise of Christ’s coming gives strength to keep going:

“Are we tried? Then the nearness of our joy whispers patience. Are we growing weary because we do not see the harvest of our seed-sowing? Again this glorious truth cries to us, ‘Be patient.’”

Charles H. Spurgeon, The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith

Until He comes

This series began with the “cloud of witnesses all around us” (Hebrews 12:1). We have met them one by one: patriarchs and prophets, apostles and martyrs, monks and mothers, reformers and revival preachers, missionaries, prisoners and ordinary believers from every continent. They were not perfect people. Many failed, and some failed badly. But they prayed, and their prayers rose before God like incense.

In the first chapter of this book we pictured the praying church as one prayer meeting, two thousand years long. Now we can see how it ends. The witnesses have finished their race. But there is a place in that meeting with your name on it. No one else can pray your prayers: for your family, your street, your church, your nation. They will go into the same golden bowls as theirs.

Each generation kept its place by teaching the next. Hannah gave Samuel to the LORD, Lois taught Eunice, and Paul told Timothy to pass on what he had heard “to trustworthy people who will be able to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). Someone taught you to pray. Now it is your turn to teach someone else, until the day the door opens and the One we have prayed to comes. Then the prayer meeting will become a feast, and the bowls of prayer will give way to songs of praise.

Three key insights

  1. The hope of Christ’s coming gives us patience to keep praying when we do not yet see the harvest. The bowls in heaven fill slowly, and the witnesses before us did not receive all they asked for. But the Lord is near, and His nearness whispers patience to weary believers.
  2. Longing for Christ to come does not take us out of the world, but sends us to pray and work for it. Brainerd’s last prayer joined “Come, Lord Jesus” with a prayer for God’s kingdom to come over all the earth. Those who love His coming love the people He came to save.
  3. Until the Lord comes, each generation takes its place in the prayer meeting and teaches the next one to pray. The cloud of witnesses has run its race. Now it is our turn to pray, in our own languages and our own places, and to hand on what we have learned.

For us today

Believers pray “Come, Lord Jesus” in very different places. For some, life is comfortable, and the prayer can feel distant. For others it is the cry of every day: a family in a refugee camp, a pastor in prison, a mother who has buried a child, a church whose building has been burned. Both need this prayer. It wakes the comfortable to long for more than this world can give. And it promises the suffering that their tears are seen and that their story does not end in the dark.

It is also a prayer the whole church can pray together. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, house church and cathedral, all say “Amen” to the last words of the Bible. Whatever divides us, we wait for the same Lord.

Try this

This week, take your place in the great prayer meeting.

  • End each day with the last prayer. Before you sleep, say Revelation 22:20, and then simply, “Come, Lord Jesus.”
  • Pray with the witnesses. Choose one person from this series each day, thank God for their life, and ask Him to give you their faith.
  • Pray for the waiting church. Name one country where believers suffer for Christ, and pray for them by name if you can, until you hear of the next.
  • Pass on the torch. Teach one younger believer, a child, a friend or a new Christian, a simple way to pray, as others taught you (2 Timothy 2:2).

A closing prayer

Lord Jesus, You are coming soon. Thank You for the great cloud of witnesses who prayed before me: for Abraham and Hannah and Daniel, for Your apostles and martyrs, for the monks and mothers, reformers and missionaries, and for every hidden believer whose prayers fill the golden bowls before Your throne. Thank You that You always live to pray for us. Give me a seat in Your prayer meeting, and keep me faithful in it. Let Your kingdom come in my home, my church and my land, and among every nation. Comfort Your suffering people while they wait. And on the day You come, gather us all, from every tribe and tongue, to see Your face. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

Questions for reflection

  • Brainerd’s last prayer joined his longing for heaven with his prayer for the world. How can longing for Christ’s coming make you more faithful today?
  • Which witnesses from this series have most changed the way you pray, and why?
  • Where is your place in the church’s great prayer meeting? Who will you pray for, and with, in the years ahead?

Read more on Ochorus

  • Charles H. Spurgeon, The Cheque Book of the Bank of Faith, especially “The Month of June”
  • Ochorus Originals, Devoted to Prayer, especially “Golden Bowls”
  • Ochorus Originals, The Fire on the Altar, especially “Praying in the Snow”

fields.title: Conclusion: The Torch Is Yours
fields.body_html:
“The smoke of the incense rose with the prayers of God’s holy people from the angel’s hand before God.” (Revelation 8:4)

We began this book in the throne room of heaven, where the elders hold bowls of gold full of incense, “the prayers of God’s holy people.” In the eighth chapter of Revelation, John sees those prayers again. An angel stands at the golden altar before the throne, the incense is added to the prayers of all God’s people, and the smoke rises before God.

Then something happens. The angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and throws it down to the earth, and there are thunder, voices and lightning (Revelation 8:5). The prayers that went up come back down as God’s action in the world. Not one of them was wasted.

That is the hope of this whole series. For eleven volumes we have watched the prayers of God’s people rise: from Abraham under the stars to believers praying tonight in a prison cell or a crowded city. We have seen many of them answered, some at once and some long after the one who prayed had died. And we have learned that the rest are kept, in bowls of gold, before the throne of God.

What the witnesses taught us

Here, in a few lines, is some of what the whole cloud of witnesses taught us about our own life of prayer:

  • Whenever we pray, we join a meeting that began long before us and has never closed its doors (chapter 1).
  • Every true prayer begins with faith that God is real and rewards those who search for Him (chapter 2).
  • God’s word gives us not only something to read but words to speak back to Him (chapter 3).
  • In every century the church has fasted, and fasting has always served prayer, never replaced it (chapter 4).
  • Praying alone teaches us to hear God, and praying together teaches us to carry one another (chapter 5).
  • Persistence keeps coming back to God Himself, while nagging only keeps coming back to the thing we want (chapter 6).
  • Even the Son of God prayed a prayer that the Father did not grant, and He was still heard (chapter 7).
  • Every piece of news from a distant land can become a call to prayer (chapter 8).
  • Revival cannot be manufactured, but God has always loved to send it to people who pray (chapter 9).
  • Prayer at home is woven into ordinary moments: at the table, on the road, at bedtime and on waking (chapter 10).
  • A rule of prayer is a help for weak people, not a prize for strong ones (chapter 11).
  • Until the Lord comes, each generation takes its place in the prayer meeting and teaches the next one to pray (chapter 12).

You will find every key insight from all eleven volumes gathered by theme in Appendix A, every Scripture in the series in Bible order in Appendix B, every witness in the order they lived in Appendix C, simple ways to pray in Appendix D, and the books on Ochorus where you can meet the witnesses for yourself in Appendix E.

What they all knew

If you could gather the whole cloud of witnesses into one room and ask them what they had learned, they would not agree on everything. They lived in different centuries, spoke different languages and belonged to different churches. But on a few things, they would speak with one voice.

They would tell you that God is real, and that He hears. They would tell you that He is a Father, and that the way to Him is open through Jesus. They would tell you that prayer is not first a technique but a friendship, and that it grows the way any friendship grows: by spending time together, day after day. They would tell you to pray with the Scriptures open, to pray alone and with others, to keep going when the answer is slow, and to trust God when it does not come. And they would tell you that they were ordinary people. Abraham bargained, Hannah wept, Elijah asked God to let him die, Peter fell asleep, and Bunyan prayed in a jail while his family struggled without him. God heard them anyway.

The torch is yours

At the end of Hebrews 11, after its long roll of the faithful, the writer says that “all these died still holding to faith. They did not receive what was promised, but they saw it from far off and welcomed it” (Hebrews 11:13). Then he turns to us: “since we too have so vast a cloud of witnesses all around us,” let us run (Hebrews 12:1).

Every volume of this series has ended by passing the torch to the next. This is the last volume, and there is no next one to pass it to. The torch is yours.

You will not carry it alone. The witnesses go before you. Your brothers and sisters around the world carry it beside you. And Jesus Himself, “the pioneer who leads the way in faith and brings it to perfection” (Hebrews 12:2), holds it with you, and prays for you still.

So take your seat in the meeting. Open the Scriptures and pray them back to God. Keep your hour. Fast, when He calls you to it. Pray in secret, and pray with others. Wait, and keep waiting. Trust Him in the silence. Pray for the nations, for your city and for your home. Ask Him to revive His church, and to begin with you. And every day, until He comes, join the oldest prayer of the church: “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

One day the meeting will end. The crowd that no one could number, “from every nation and from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9), will stand together before the throne. Abraham will be there, and Hannah, and the apostles, the martyrs and the monks, the reformers and the missionaries, the praying grandmothers and the prisoners who sang. And if you have trusted in Jesus, you will be there too. On that day, prayer will become praise, and we will see the One we have prayed to face to face.

Until then, there is still room in the bowls for your prayers.

A closing prayer

Our Father in heaven, thank You for the great cloud of witnesses: for the patriarchs and prophets, for Jesus our Lord, who prayed for us and prays for us still, for the apostles and martyrs, the monks and mystics, the reformers and the Puritans, the missionaries and the revivalists, and for Your praying church in every nation today. Thank You that not one of their prayers was lost. Teach me to pray as they prayed. Give me a place in the meeting, and keep me faithful in it all my days. Let my prayers rise before You like incense, with all the prayers of Your holy people. And bring us all, from every tribe and tongue, into Your presence, where faith will become sight and prayer will become praise.

“Now to the one who is able to guard you from stumbling, and to bring you into the presence of His glory without blemish and rejoicing greatly, to God alone, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, might, and authority, before time began, now, and for all the ages to come. Amen.” (Jude 1:24-25)

Come, Lord Jesus. Amen.

fields.title: Appendix A: Key Insights from the Whole Series
fields.body_html:
Every chapter of every volume closes with three key insights. Here they are all gathered by theme, each pointing back to its volume and chapter and to that chapter’s key verse.

The Father’s Love

  • God’s glory is His goodness, and we see it most clearly in Jesus. Vol. 1, ch. 4, “Let Me See Your Glory” (Exodus 33:18)
  • The best thing we can ask of God is God Himself. Vol. 1, ch. 7, One Thing I Ask (Psalm 27:4)
  • No one has fallen too far to come home to God. Vol. 1, ch. 8, A Pure Heart (Psalm 51:10)
  • Prayer begins with relationship, not requests. Vol. 2, ch. 4, Our Father in Heaven (Matthew 6:9-10)
  • The secret room is a meeting, not a ritual. Vol. 2, ch. 6, The Secret Room (Matthew 6:6)
  • We do not pray to wear God down. Vol. 2, ch. 8, Always Pray and Never Give Up (Luke 18:1)
  • The Father Himself loves us. Vol. 2, ch. 15, Asking in His Name (John 16:24)
  • We can die, and live, in trust. Vol. 2, ch. 19, Prayers from the Cross (Luke 23:34)
  • God remembers every sincere prayer. Vol. 3, ch. 7, Prayers That Rose Before God (Acts 10:4)
  • God is never too busy for His children. Vol. 3, ch. 17, Never Stop Praying (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18)
  • We call God “Father” only because His Spirit gives us the right. Vol. 4, ch. 8, Why We Say “Our” Father (Galatians 4:6)
  • God leads us into quiet places to speak tenderly to us, not to punish us. Vol. 4, ch. 9, Into the Desert to Pray (Hosea 2:14)
  • We pray not to inform God but to become His close friends. Vol. 4, ch. 14, Prayer, the Light of the Soul (Psalm 18:28)
  • We were made for God, and our hearts find rest only in Him. Vol. 4, ch. 16, “Our Heart Is Restless” (Psalm 62:1)
  • Even the best minds must ask God to teach them how to seek Him. Vol. 5, ch. 6, Faith Seeking Your Face (Psalm 27:7-8)
  • Our love for God is always an answer to His love for us. Vol. 5, ch. 7, Jesus, the Very Thought of You (1 John 4:19)
  • God holds all things, even the smallest, because He loves them. Vol. 5, ch. 13, “All Shall Be Well” (Romans 8:28)
  • Prayer is a friendship with Jesus, kept alive by frequent and honest conversation. Vol. 6, ch. 6, Prayer as Friendship (John 15:15)
  • We can work carefully without working anxiously, because our Father holds our hand. Vol. 6, ch. 9, Prayer for Busy People (Colossians 3:17)
  • Christ does not throw away bruised people; He bends down to mend them. Vol. 6, ch. 13, The Bruised Reed (Isaiah 42:3)
  • God is a Father to orphans, and He loves to meet their needs through people who pray. Vol. 7, ch. 3, An Orphanage Built on Prayer (Psalm 68:5)
  • Thirst for God is not a sign of failure but an invitation to come and drink. Vol. 8, ch. 4, My Soul Thirsts for You (Psalm 63:1)
  • Anyone may come to God as a child comes to a father, without priest, journey or sacrifice. Vol. 8, ch. 16, A Bishop on His Knees (Psalm 72:8)
  • The way into God’s kingdom is not climbing up but being carried, as a child is carried by her father. Vol. 8, ch. 19, The Little Way (Matthew 18:3)
  • God pours out His Spirit on those whom the world overlooks, and He makes them messengers of His word. Vol. 9, ch. 2, Your Daughters Will Prophesy (Joel 2:28)
  • Christ meets those who honestly cry out to Him, even those who once fought against Him. Vol. 9, ch. 7, Prayer Is Breathing (Psalm 16:11)
  • The new birth turns set phrases into the prayer of a child speaking to a Father. Vol. 9, ch. 12, Prayer Bands Across Asia (Acts 3:19-20)
  • Hearing the Shepherd’s voice begins with belonging to the Shepherd. Vol. 10, ch. 11, My Sheep Hear My Voice (John 10:27)
  • God’s house is meant to be a house of prayer where every people and every outsider is welcome. Vol. 10, ch. 12, Fresh Wind, Fresh Fire (Isaiah 56:7)
  • True prayer holds together awe before a great King and the closeness of a child with a Father. Vol. 10, ch. 20, Awe and Intimacy (Psalm 63:3)
  • The Great God is a Father, and we come to Him through Jesus, not through a long road of our own making. Vol. 11, ch. 2, What the Witnesses Agree On (Hebrews 11:6)
  • A fast kept for the Father’s eyes alone is a secret He delights to reward. Vol. 11, ch. 4, Prayer and Fasting (Matthew 6:17-18)
  • Intercession for the world rests on the one Mediator who gave Himself for all. Vol. 11, ch. 8, For All People (1 Timothy 2:3-4)

Learning to Pray

  • The best prayer asks for God Himself, not only for His gifts. Vol. 1, ch. 4, “Let Me See Your Glory” (Exodus 33:18)
  • A single desire gives our prayers focus and strength. Vol. 1, ch. 7, One Thing I Ask (Psalm 27:4)
  • Scripture stored in the heart becomes prayer in the dark. Vol. 1, ch. 13, A Prayer from the Depths (Jonah 2:2)
  • A short prayer in the moment is real prayer, and God hears it. Vol. 1, ch. 15, Arrow Prayers and Long Fasts (Nehemiah 2:4-5)
  • Prayer can be learned. Vol. 2, ch. 3, “Lord, Teach Us to Pray” (Luke 11:1)
  • We learn to pray by watching people who pray. Vol. 2, ch. 3, “Lord, Teach Us to Pray” (Luke 11:1)
  • Jesus is a willing teacher. Vol. 2, ch. 3, “Lord, Teach Us to Pray” (Luke 11:1)
  • Scripture gives us words when we are afraid. Vol. 3, ch. 4, “Sovereign Master”: Praying Under Threat (Acts 4:31)
  • Not knowing what to pray is not a failure; it is where the Spirit’s help begins. Vol. 3, ch. 14, When We Do Not Know What to Pray (Romans 8:26)
  • The Lord’s Prayer is a pattern to live inside, not a formula to rush through. Vol. 4, ch. 1, Three Times a Day (Psalm 55:17)
  • The heart must be lifted before the hands. Vol. 4, ch. 7, Prayer Rising Like Incense (Psalm 141:2)
  • Prayer is learned from those who walked the road before us. Vol. 4, ch. 11, “God, Come and Rescue Me” (Psalm 70:1)
  • What we sing, we remember, and what we remember shapes what we believe. Vol. 4, ch. 13, Prayer in Song (Colossians 3:16)
  • We do not need a loud voice or a quiet room for God to hear us. Vol. 4, ch. 14, Prayer, the Light of the Soul (Psalm 18:28)
  • The prayers of others can give us words when our own words fail. Vol. 5, ch. 5, Out of the Depths (Psalm 130:1-4)
  • Faith and careful thinking are friends, and both can lead us to prayer. Vol. 5, ch. 6, Faith Seeking Your Face (Psalm 27:7-8)
  • We become like the One we look at. Vol. 5, ch. 9, Gazing on Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18)
  • One short word of love from the heart can pierce heaven. Vol. 5, ch. 11, A Simple Reaching for God (Psalm 73:25)
  • Having God’s word is not enough; we need Him to open our eyes to it. Vol. 5, ch. 15, Open My Eyes to Your Word (Psalm 119:18)
  • Prayer is not only speaking to God but also listening for His voice. Vol. 5, ch. 17, “Speak, for Your Servant Is Listening” (1 Samuel 3:10)
  • The simple words we learned as children can become a lifelong school of prayer. Vol. 6, ch. 2, A Simple Way to Pray (Psalm 1:2)
  • God wants us to pray with our minds as well as our hearts, in words we understand. Vol. 6, ch. 4, Praying with the Mind Also (1 Corinthians 14:15)
  • In prayer, loving much matters more than thinking much. Vol. 6, ch. 6, Prayer as Friendship (John 15:15)
  • True devotion fits our calling and makes us better at it. Vol. 6, ch. 9, Prayer for Busy People (Colossians 3:17)
  • A life of prayer can be built from God’s own words, gathered one by one. Vol. 6, ch. 11, At Midnight I Rise (Psalm 119:62)
  • Prayer is a way to taste God’s goodness, not only to talk about it. Vol. 6, ch. 12, Taste and See (Psalm 34:8)
  • We learn to pray by praying, so we must be patient with ourselves and with others. Vol. 6, ch. 13, The Bruised Reed (Isaiah 42:3)
  • Meditation turns truths we know into joys we feel. Vol. 6, ch. 14, Set Your Mind on Things Above (Colossians 3:1-2)
  • Prayer is pouring out the heart to God, not putting on a show of fine words. Vol. 6, ch. 15, A Heart Without Words (Psalm 62:8)
  • Prayer is the heart turning to God, so even the simplest believer can pray. Vol. 7, ch. 1, Be Still and Know (Psalm 46:10)
  • Children learn to pray when they see prayer kept faithfully at home. Vol. 7, ch. 6, The Apron over Her Head (Psalm 31:20)
  • A true believer needs prayer as a living body needs breath. Vol. 7, ch. 8, Oh, That You Would Tear the Heavens (Isaiah 64:1)
  • Prayer grows wider when we remember the whole church and the whole world, not only our own congregation. Vol. 7, ch. 16, The Prayer Call of 1784 (Isaiah 54:2)
  • Bold asking grows best from deep reading of God’s Word. Vol. 8, ch. 5, Open Your Mouth Wide (Psalm 81:10)
  • Unceasing prayer is learned slowly, with a patient teacher beside us. Vol. 8, ch. 6, A Pilgrim Learns to Pray Without Ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17)
  • Prayer is a way to receive the Holy Spirit, not a way to earn God’s favor. Vol. 8, ch. 7, A Peaceful Spirit (Isaiah 26:3)
  • God’s words living in us teach us what to ask, so we should listen before we speak. Vol. 8, ch. 17, Abide in Me (John 15:7)
  • The longing for God is itself a gift we may ask God to give. Vol. 9, ch. 20, The Pursuit of God (Psalm 42:1)
  • A short prayer, repeated slowly, can carry a whole heart to God. Vol. 10, ch. 4, Living Together in Unity (Psalm 133:1)
  • God does not need long or polished prayers, and short, simple prayers from ordinary believers are welcome before Him. Vol. 10, ch. 8, What Happens When Women Pray (Jeremiah 33:3)
  • God’s word cannot be chained, even when His servants are. Vol. 10, ch. 9, More Persecution, More Growth (2 Corinthians 4:8-9)
  • A wise fast fits the body and the season of life that God has given us. Vol. 10, ch. 10, The Fast God Chooses (Isaiah 58:6)
  • What we believe we have heard from God must be tested by His written word and by His people. Vol. 10, ch. 11, My Sheep Hear My Voice (John 10:27)
  • A new season of prayer often begins with the honest confession that we do not pray as we should. Vol. 10, ch. 15, The Fire Is Lit Again (Leviticus 6:13)
  • It is never too late to discover prayer, and hard seasons are often where we find it. Vol. 10, ch. 20, Awe and Intimacy (Psalm 63:3)
  • God’s word gives us not only something to read but words to speak back to Him. Vol. 11, ch. 3, Prayer and the Word (Psalm 119:18)
  • Persistence keeps coming back to God Himself, while nagging only keeps coming back to the thing we want. Vol. 11, ch. 6, Waiting on the Lord (Isaiah 40:31)
  • Every piece of news from a distant land can become a call to prayer. Vol. 11, ch. 8, For All People (1 Timothy 2:3-4)
  • God’s words must live in our own hearts before we can pass them on at home. Vol. 11, ch. 10, The Family Altar (Deuteronomy 6:6-7)
  • A rule of prayer is a help for weak people, not a prize for strong ones. Vol. 11, ch. 11, A Rule of Prayer (Psalm 92:1-2)
  • Until the Lord comes, each generation takes its place in the prayer meeting and teaches the next one to pray. Vol. 11, ch. 12, “Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20)

Making Room for Prayer

  • The more we know God, the more we long to know Him. Vol. 1, ch. 4, “Let Me See Your Glory” (Exodus 33:18)
  • The habit of prayer we build in quiet days carries us through dangerous ones. Vol. 1, ch. 14, Windows Open Toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10)
  • If Jesus needed to pray, so do we. Vol. 2, ch. 1, Very Early in the Morning (Mark 1:35)
  • Busyness is a reason to pray, not an excuse not to. Vol. 2, ch. 1, Very Early in the Morning (Mark 1:35)
  • God’s concerns come first. Vol. 2, ch. 4, Our Father in Heaven (Matthew 6:9-10)
  • Prayer is for an audience of One. Vol. 2, ch. 6, The Secret Room (Matthew 6:6)
  • What happens in secret shapes our public life. Vol. 2, ch. 6, The Secret Room (Matthew 6:6)
  • We need both the secret room and the prayer meeting. Vol. 2, ch. 11, Where Two or Three Agree (Matthew 18:19-20)
  • Prayer was one of the four things the first church would not let go. Vol. 3, ch. 2, Devoted to the Prayers (Acts 2:42)
  • Set times of prayer help us keep praying. Vol. 3, ch. 3, The Hour of Prayer (Acts 3:1)
  • Prayer is real work, and it needs protected time. Vol. 3, ch. 5, Holding Fast to Prayer (Acts 6:4)
  • Good work can crowd out prayer as easily as bad work. Vol. 3, ch. 5, Holding Fast to Prayer (Acts 6:4)
  • Fasting is prayer with the whole person. Vol. 3, ch. 9, Worship, Fasting and Sending (Acts 13:2-3)
  • God loves to meet people at the places where they faithfully pray. Vol. 3, ch. 10, The Place of Prayer by the River (Acts 16:13)
  • Praying without stopping is for ordinary working people. Vol. 3, ch. 17, Never Stop Praying (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18)
  • A simple rhythm of prayer can carry a whole life. Vol. 4, ch. 1, Three Times a Day (Psalm 55:17)
  • A soldier keeps watch at set times, and so should we. Vol. 4, ch. 6, Prayer, the Wall of Faith (Ephesians 6:18)
  • Our whole life can become one long prayer. Vol. 4, ch. 7, Prayer Rising Like Incense (Psalm 141:2)
  • Time alone with God makes us more useful to others, not less. Vol. 4, ch. 9, Into the Desert to Pray (Hosea 2:14)
  • One short verse can carry us through the whole day. Vol. 4, ch. 11, “God, Come and Rescue Me” (Psalm 70:1)
  • Any home can become a house of prayer. Vol. 4, ch. 12, A Home Made a House of Prayer (Psalm 31:5)
  • Calling on the name of Jesus is a prayer for every place and every hour. Vol. 4, ch. 18, Lord Jesus Christ, Have Mercy (Luke 18:38)
  • Praise offered seven times a day teaches us that the whole day belongs to God. Vol. 5, ch. 1, Ora et Labora: Pray and Work (Psalm 119:164)
  • Fasting together, as a whole church, teaches us that we need God more than food. Vol. 5, ch. 2, Ethiopia Stretches Out Her Hands (Psalm 68:31)
  • No part of an ordinary day is too small to bring to God in prayer. Vol. 5, ch. 4, The Prayers of Ordinary Days (Psalm 121:8)
  • To meet God we must sometimes shut the door on our cares for a while. Vol. 5, ch. 6, Faith Seeking Your Face (Psalm 27:7-8)
  • A hidden life of prayer is never a wasted life. Vol. 5, ch. 9, Gazing on Christ (2 Corinthians 3:18)
  • Before we study about God, we should speak to God. Vol. 5, ch. 10, A Prayer Before Study (James 1:5)
  • Stillness before God is not empty but full of His presence. Vol. 5, ch. 12, Waiting in Stillness (Lamentations 3:25-26)
  • The busier the day ahead, the more it needs to begin with God. Vol. 6, ch. 1, Too Busy Not to Pray (Psalm 46:1)
  • Thinking ahead in prayer about the people we will meet helps us meet them with gentleness. Vol. 6, ch. 9, Prayer for Busy People (Colossians 3:17)
  • We can keep up a quiet conversation with God while our hands are busy. Vol. 6, ch. 16, Among the Pots and Pans (Psalm 16:8)
  • A few words of Scripture, read slowly, can feed the soul more than many words read in a hurry. Vol. 7, ch. 1, Be Still and Know (Psalm 46:10)
  • A crowded, noisy home can still hold a hidden place for meeting God. Vol. 7, ch. 6, The Apron over Her Head (Psalm 31:20)
  • Prayer with others must grow from prayer alone with God. Vol. 7, ch. 9, A Concert of Prayer (Zechariah 8:21)
  • The best hours of the day belong to God, not only the hours left over. Vol. 8, ch. 4, My Soul Thirsts for You (Psalm 63:1)
  • A short prayer, prayed again and again, can move from the lips into the heart. Vol. 8, ch. 6, A Pilgrim Learns to Pray Without Ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:17)
  • Even a crowded working day has room for God when someone opens a door at noon. Vol. 8, ch. 8, The Noon Prayer Meeting (2 Chronicles 7:14)
  • Prayer grows strong through daily practice, as a soldier grows strong through daily drill. Vol. 8, ch. 14, Knee Drill (Isaiah 61:1)
  • The hours before dawn, given to God, can shape a whole life and outlast it. Vol. 8, ch. 20, God Looked for an Intercessor (Isaiah 59:16)
  • Like a sea creature rising for air, we must keep coming up to God in prayer if we are to live in a drowning world. Vol. 9, ch. 7, Prayer Is Breathing (Psalm 16:11)
  • Learning to pray in quiet days prepares us to pray in dark ones. Vol. 9, ch. 14, My Times Are in Your Hand (Psalm 31:15)
  • The busiest life still needs unhurried time alone with God. Vol. 9, ch. 20, The Pursuit of God (Psalm 42:1)
  • Shared silence before God is a prayer that needs no common language. Vol. 10, ch. 4, Living Together in Unity (Psalm 133:1)
  • Time given to God is never stolen from the needy, because it is where the strength to serve them is found. Vol. 10, ch. 5, Prayer Gives a Clean Heart (Matthew 25:40)
  • Going apart to a quiet place helps us give God our whole attention. Vol. 10, ch. 6, I Look Up to the Mountains (Psalm 121:1-2)
  • Fasting does not earn God’s answer; it humbles us so that we can seek Him with our whole heart. Vol. 10, ch. 10, The Fast God Chooses (Isaiah 58:6)
  • The hours we would give to sleep can become a gift we bring to God. Vol. 10, ch. 17, All Night Before God (Luke 6:12)
  • Reading that turns into prayer feeds our own soul before it feeds anyone else. Vol. 11, ch. 3, Prayer and the Word (Psalm 119:18)
  • In every century the church has fasted, and fasting has always served prayer, never replaced it. Vol. 11, ch. 4, Prayer and Fasting (Matthew 6:17-18)
  • The habit of secret prayer and the habit of shared prayer each protect the other from its own dangers. Vol. 11, ch. 5, Alone and Together (Acts 12:12)
  • Prayer at home is woven into ordinary moments: at the table, on the road, at bedtime and on waking. Vol. 11, ch. 10, The Family Altar (Deuteronomy 6:6-7)

Asking Boldly

  • We can pray boldly because we pray to a God who is just and good. Vol. 1, ch. 1, The Friend Who Pleaded for a City (Genesis 18:25)
  • The strongest prayers appeal to God’s own character, name and promises. Vol. 1, ch. 3, Standing in the Gap (Exodus 32:11)
  • The best prayers ask God to make Himself known. Vol. 1, ch. 10, Fire from Heaven, Rain on the Earth (1 Kings 18:37)
  • Pray for the answer that will make God known. Vol. 1, ch. 12, Opening the Letter Before the Lord (2 Kings 19:14-15)
  • God cares about our daily needs. Vol. 2, ch. 5, Bread, Forgiveness, Deliverance (Matthew 6:11-13)
  • God invites us to ask boldly. Vol. 2, ch. 7, Ask, Seek, Knock (Luke 11:9)
  • We come to God on Jesus’ credit, not our own. Vol. 2, ch. 15, Asking in His Name (John 16:24)
  • God is able to do far beyond anything we ask or think. Vol. 3, ch. 13, Rooted Deep in Love (Ephesians 3:16-19)
  • The prayers of God’s people move heaven, and heaven moves the earth. Vol. 3, ch. 20, Golden Bowls (Revelation 8:3-4)
  • Even a new believer may come to God with bold confidence. Vol. 4, ch. 5, Prayer in a Prison Cell (Psalm 23:4)
  • God gives wisdom gladly to everyone who asks Him in faith. Vol. 5, ch. 10, A Prayer Before Study (James 1:5)
  • We can speak the truth boldly to leaders when we have first prayed for them humbly. Vol. 5, ch. 14, Giving God No Rest (Isaiah 62:6-7)
  • God has chosen to do His work in answer to the prayers of His people. Vol. 7, ch. 7, “God Does Nothing but in Answer to Prayer” (James 4:2)
  • We may boldly ask God to come down in power where people have been forgotten. Vol. 7, ch. 8, Oh, That You Would Tear the Heavens (Isaiah 64:1)
  • Hunger for God’s word, spoken aloud by ordinary believers, is often where a work of God begins. Vol. 7, ch. 11, Revive Your Work (Habakkuk 3:2)
  • Because we come to a generous King, we may bring Him large requests. Vol. 7, ch. 13, Ask Large Petitions (Ephesians 3:20-21)
  • We may bring God the plain needs of life and death as members of His family. Vol. 8, ch. 3, A Covenant with God (Jeremiah 50:5)
  • The God who has already rescued us invites us to open our mouths wide. Vol. 8, ch. 5, Open Your Mouth Wide (Psalm 81:10)
  • We may ask God for definite things, because He meets every need from His own great wealth. Vol. 8, ch. 11, Move Man Through God (Philippians 4:19)
  • A wide prayer for the nations can be prayed by a humble heart. Vol. 8, ch. 16, A Bishop on His Knees (Psalm 72:8)
  • The prayers God loves to answer grow out of staying close to Jesus, as fruit grows on a branch. Vol. 8, ch. 17, Abide in Me (John 15:7)
  • The Spirit comes to people who wait for Him in prayer, and He gives power so that they can bear witness to Jesus. Vol. 9, ch. 3, A Stable on Azusa Street (Acts 1:8)
  • The church’s greatest work is to ask God boldly for what He Himself wants done on earth. Vol. 9, ch. 13, The Prayer Ministry of the Church (Matthew 18:18)
  • The simple prayers of children can teach adults to trust. Vol. 10, ch. 2, Before They Call, I Will Answer (Isaiah 65:24)
  • The God who opens blind eyes can also close watching eyes, and we may ask Him to protect His word. Vol. 10, ch. 3, Prayer That Opens Closed Doors (Revelation 3:8)
  • When we are weak and out of answers, calling on God together is not our last resort but our first work. Vol. 10, ch. 12, Fresh Wind, Fresh Fire (Isaiah 56:7)

Persistence

  • Humble persistence is welcome in God’s presence. Vol. 1, ch. 1, The Friend Who Pleaded for a City (Genesis 18:25)
  • Sometimes we prevail in prayer through weakness, not strength. Vol. 1, ch. 2, “I Will Not Let You Go” (Genesis 32:26)
  • Keep praying and keep looking until the small cloud appears. Vol. 1, ch. 10, Fire from Heaven, Rain on the Earth (1 Kings 18:37)

  • A child’s prayer can be bold, because it trusts the Father’s mercy more than its own goodness. Vol. 8, ch. 19, The Little Way (Matthew 18:3)
  • God is still looking for people who will stand between Him and a needy world in prayer. Vol. 8, ch. 20, God Looked for an Intercessor (Isaiah 59:16)
  • Even those whom God uses greatly are clay pots, and they need care, rest and our prayers. Vol. 9, ch. 1, “Bend Me” (Ephesians 5:18)
  • Praying by name for many people is a work that ordinary believers can share. Vol. 9, ch. 2, Your Daughters Will Prophesy (Joel 2:28)
  • Tears shed in prayer for others are seeds that God will one day turn into a harvest of joy. Vol. 9, ch. 6, Sowing in Tears (Psalm 126:5-6)
  • When we pray for children at risk, we share both the anger and the welcome of Jesus. Vol. 9, ch. 8, Let the Children Come (Mark 10:14)
  • Standing in the gap means letting another’s need become our own burden before God. Vol. 9, ch. 10, Standing in the Gap for a World at War (Ezekiel 22:30)
  • No one is too old, too weak or too hidden to pray for revival. Vol. 9, ch. 18, Two Old Sisters on Lewis (Isaiah 44:3)
  • We can pray for workers God has not yet called, and He may already be preparing them. Vol. 9, ch. 19, The Praying Men of Charlotte (Isaiah 55:11)
  • When we pray for the nations, God may ask us to be part of His answer. Vol. 10, ch. 1, Ask of Me, and I Will Give You the Nations (Psalm 2:8)
  • Small and weak churches are precious to Christ, and He sends others to strengthen them. Vol. 10, ch. 3, Prayer That Opens Closed Doors (Revelation 3:8)
  • To bless a persecutor is to ask God for their greatest good, and the greatest good of all is repentance. Vol. 10, ch. 7, Bless Those Who Persecute You (Romans 12:14)
  • Prayer for the world becomes faithful when it learns the names of the peoples in it. Vol. 10, ch. 13, The 10/40 Window (Revelation 7:9)
  • To pray for a city is to want good for all its people, not only growth for our own church. Vol. 10, ch. 14, Pray for the Peace of the City (Jeremiah 29:7)
  • God’s kingdom comes into the world one heart at a time, so we may pray for it by name. Vol. 10, ch. 16, Your Kingdom Come (Matthew 6:10)
  • Remembering prisoners means praying as if their chains were on our own wrists. Vol. 10, ch. 18, Prayer in a Shipping Container (Hebrews 13:3)
  • Standing with a suffering brother, in prayer and in public, is love that may cost us dearly. Vol. 10, ch. 19, Not Bowing to the Image (Daniel 3:17-18)
  • A home that is known as a place of prayer becomes a refuge for those in trouble. Vol. 11, ch. 5, Alone and Together (Acts 12:12)
  • A believer who prays faithfully for one far-off worker shares in the harvest that worker gathers. Vol. 11, ch. 8, For All People (1 Timothy 2:3-4)
  • Every believer has a household to pray for, whether married or single, with children or without. Vol. 11, ch. 10, The Family Altar (Deuteronomy 6:6-7)
  • Longing for Christ to come does not take us out of the world, but sends us to pray and work for it. Vol. 11, ch. 12, “Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20)

Christ Who Prays for Us

  • True intercession costs the one who prays. Vol. 1, ch. 3, Standing in the Gap (Exodus 32:11)
  • Jesus never stops praying for us, so we need never stop praying for others. Vol. 1, ch. 6, The Sin of Not Praying (1 Samuel 12:23)
  • Jesus Himself prayed the laments, so we never pray them alone. Vol. 1, ch. 16, “How Long, LORD?” Honest Prayer (Psalm 13:1)
  • Jesus prays for us by name, even before we fall. Vol. 2, ch. 16, “I Have Prayed for You” (Luke 22:31-32)
  • Restored people strengthen others. Vol. 2, ch. 16, “I Have Prayed for You” (Luke 22:31-32)
  • Jesus prayed for you before you were born. Vol. 2, ch. 17, That They May All Be One (John 17:21)
  • Jesus is still praying for us. Vol. 2, ch. 20, He Always Lives to Pray for Us (Hebrews 7:25)
  • Our salvation rests on His prayers, not our strength. Vol. 2, ch. 20, He Always Lives to Pray for Us (Hebrews 7:25)
  • Our prayers are joined to His. Vol. 2, ch. 20, He Always Lives to Pray for Us (Hebrews 7:25)
  • The Holy Spirit prays for us, and the Son prays for us too. Vol. 3, ch. 14, When We Do Not Know What to Pray (Romans 8:26)
  • When we pray, Christ prays with us. Vol. 4, ch. 7, Prayer Rising Like Incense (Psalm 141:2)
  • When we do not know how to pray, the Spirit prays within us. Vol. 4, ch. 17, Christ Be with Me (Matthew 28:20)
  • Because Jesus is our high priest, the throne we approach is a throne of grace. Vol. 6, ch. 3, The Principal Exercise of Faith (Hebrews 4:16)
  • A weak and confused prayer that comes from a true desire is precious to God. Vol. 6, ch. 13, The Bruised Reed (Isaiah 42:3)
  • We can stand in the gap for others because Jesus has already stood there for us. Vol. 8, ch. 20, God Looked for an Intercessor (Isaiah 59:16)
  • Our eyes belong on Jesus, who leads the whole meeting and prays for us still. Vol. 11, ch. 1, One Prayer Meeting, Two Thousand Years Long (Hebrews 12:1)

fields.title: Appendix C: Timeline
fields.body_html:
Every person and movement in the series on one line, in the order of their times. Dates are as each chapter gives them, most of them approximate.

  • c. 2000 BC: Abraham, Mamre, near Hebron (Canaan). Vol. 1, ch. 1, The Friend Who Pleaded for a City
  • c. 1850 BC: Jacob, The Jabbok River, east of the Jordan. Vol. 1, ch. 2, “I Will Not Let You Go”
  • c. 1400s or 1200s BC (debated): Moses, Mount Sinai. Vol. 1, ch. 3, Standing in the Gap
  • c. 1400s or 1200s BC (debated): Moses, Mount Sinai. Vol. 1, ch. 4, “Let Me See Your Glory”
  • c. 1100 BC: Hannah, Shiloh, hill country of Ephraim. Vol. 1, ch. 5, Pouring Out the Soul

fields.title: Appendix D: Prayer Methods Toolkit
fields.body_html:
The witnesses in this series prayed in many ways, and some of their ways are simple enough for anyone to learn. Here are eighteen of them. None is a rule, and none makes God hear us: He hears us because of Jesus, not because of our method. Try one at a time, keep what helps, and follow the pointers to read the full stories in this series.

Praying the Psalms

The Psalms are the prayer book God gave His people, and every age of the church has prayed them. David’s laments teach us to bring God our real feelings (Volume 1, chapter 16). Benedict built his monks’ day around the Psalms (Volume 5, chapter 1), Luther warmed his cold heart with his little book of psalms (Volume 6, chapter 2), and Bonhoeffer called them the prayer book of the Bible (Volume 9, chapter 14).

  1. Choose one psalm. Psalms 23, 27, 51, 63, 103 and 139 are good places to begin.
  2. Read it slowly, aloud if you can.
  3. Stop at a line that speaks to you, and turn it into your own words to God.
  4. Tomorrow, go on to the next psalm.

Do not skip the sad psalms: “How long, LORD?” (Psalm 13:1) is a prayer of faith.

Praying the Lord’s Prayer phrase by phrase

Jesus gave His disciples a short prayer as a pattern (Volume 2, chapters 4 and 5). The Didache told new believers to pray it three times a day (Volume 4, chapter 1), and Cyprian taught why we say “our” Father (Volume 4, chapter 8). Many believers pray it slowly, one line at a time, letting each line open into their own prayers.

  1. “Our Father in heaven, may Your name be kept holy” (Matthew 6:9). Thank God that He is your Father, and praise Him.
  2. “May Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10). Pray for His rule in your home, your church, your town and the nations.
  3. “Give us today the bread we need” (Matthew 6:11). Bring Him today’s needs, yours and others’.
  4. “Forgive us what we owe You” (Matthew 6:12). Confess your sins, and forgive those who have wronged you.
  5. “Do not lead us into testing, but rescue us from the evil one” (Matthew 6:13). Ask Him to protect you and those you love.

If you have only five minutes, pray one line well.

Luther’s four strands

When Peter the barber asked Martin Luther how to pray, Luther wrote him a little book, A Simple Way to Pray (Volume 6, chapter 2). Take one line of the Lord’s Prayer, one commandment or one line of the Creed, he said, and weave it into a garland of four strands. It needs no library, only words of Scripture carried in the memory.

  1. Choose one short line, such as “Give us today the bread we need.”
  2. Instruction: What is God teaching me here?
  3. Thanksgiving: What can I thank Him for?
  4. Confession: What sin does this show me?
  5. Prayer: What shall I ask, for myself and for others?

Lectio: reading Scripture slowly into prayer

Lectio is Latin for “reading.” Benedict’s monks shared their day between prayer, work and reading the Scriptures (Volume 5, chapter 1). George Müller found that this changed his mornings (Volume 8, chapter 5). Instead of beginning the day with wandering prayer, he began by reading the Bible slowly, verse by verse, to feed his soul, and after a few minutes his reading turned, almost by itself, into prayer.

  1. Pray first: “Take the veil from my eyes, so that I may see the wonders in Your instruction” (Psalm 119:18).
  2. Read a few verses only, slowly.
  3. At each verse ask: What does this say about God? What does it say to me?
  4. Let the verse lead you into thanks, confession, asking or prayer for others.
  5. Carry one phrase through the day, and repeat it quietly to yourself (Psalm 1:2).

Read little, and meet God in it. Chapter 3 of this book, “Prayer and the Word,” says more.

The examen

Ignatius of Loyola taught a short daily prayer he called the General Examen (Volume 6, chapter 8). It is a walk back through the day with God, and he said that simple exercises like it suit even those who cannot read.

  1. Give thanks. Name three good gifts from today, and thank God for each.
  2. Ask for light. Pray, “God, look deep into me and know my heart” (Psalm 139:23).
  3. Look back. Walk through the day. Where were you near to God? Where did you turn from Him in thought, word or deed?
  4. Ask forgiveness. Confess what you have seen, and receive Christ’s forgiveness.
  5. Begin again. Ask His help for one thing tomorrow. End with the Lord’s Prayer.

Thanks comes first: the examen is not a courtroom. Ten minutes before sleep are enough.

The Jesus Prayer

Believers in the deserts of Egypt and Palestine joined two cries from the Gospels, the blind man’s “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” (Luke 18:38) and the tax collector’s “God, be merciful to me, the sinner!” (Luke 18:13). From them came the Jesus Prayer (Volume 4, chapter 18). It became the heart of Orthodox prayer, as we saw with the monks of Mount Athos (Volume 5, chapter 12) and a Russian pilgrim (Volume 8, chapter 6).

  1. Sit quietly and pray gently: “Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.”
  2. Some pray it with their breathing, or with a prayer rope, a cord of knots.
  3. When your mind wanders, come back without scolding yourself.
  4. Through the day, pray it again whenever you remember.

There is no magic in it. It is a beggar’s cry to a Savior who stops for beggars.

Arrow prayers

An arrow prayer is a short prayer sent up silently in the middle of life. When the king asked Nehemiah what he wanted, “I prayed to the God of heaven” (Nehemiah 2:4), and then he answered (Volume 1, chapter 15). In Volume 4, chapter 11, John Cassian learned from the desert teachers to pray one verse all day: “God, come and rescue me! LORD, be quick to help me!” (Psalm 70:1). On Iona and in the Scottish Highlands, believers blessed their milk, their fires and their journeys with short prayers (Volume 5, chapter 4).

  1. Learn one short verse by heart, such as Psalm 70:1.
  2. Pray it in the moment: before a hard conversation, in traffic, when fear or temptation comes, and when joy comes too.
  3. Bless ordinary tasks as you begin them: “Lord, bless this meal, this work, this journey.”

Arrow prayers fly far from a life of longer prayer, as Nehemiah’s did.

Set hours of prayer

David prayed “at evening, at morning and at noon” (Psalm 55:17), and Daniel knelt three times a day (Volume 1, chapter 14). In Volume 3, chapter 3, Peter and John went to the temple “for the afternoon prayer at three o’clock” (Acts 3:1). The Didache told new believers to pray the Lord’s Prayer three times a day (Volume 4, chapter 1), and Benedict’s monks stopped their work to pray seven times a day (Volume 5, chapter 1).

  1. Choose two or three times: morning, midday and evening is the oldest pattern.
  2. Tie each to something you already do, such as waking, eating or going to bed.
  3. Keep each time short: a psalm, the Lord’s Prayer, a few words of your own.
  4. If you miss one, do not give up. Pray at the next.

The hours do not wall prayer in; they turn the whole day toward God.

Dawn prayer

Jesus rose “long before daylight” to pray (Mark 1:35), and the psalmist said, “LORD, at daybreak You hear my voice” (Psalm 5:3). In Pyongyang, the elder Kil Sun-ju opened the church before dawn to everyone who wanted to pray, and Korean churches around the world still meet before sunrise (Volume 9, chapter 5).

  1. Go to bed a little earlier, and rise before your household or work begins.
  2. Sing or read a psalm, read a few verses, and pray for the day ahead.
  3. If you can, meet with other believers at dawn, at church or in a home.

Dawn prayer is a gift, not a test. If illness, night work or small children make it impossible, God hears you at every hour.

Praying aloud together

In January 1907, in Pyongyang, more than a thousand men prayed aloud at the same time, each in his own words (Volume 9, chapter 4). Koreans call this tongsŏng kido. Believers at Mukti in India (Volume 9, chapter 2) and in Africa’s night vigils (Volume 10, chapter 17) have prayed in the same way.

  1. Agree on what to pray for: one need, one person or your town.
  2. At the leader’s word, everyone prays aloud at once, each in his or her own words and language.
  3. After some minutes the leader closes with a short prayer, and all say “Amen.”

This helps shy people, because no one listens to them alone.

A concert of prayer

In the 1700s a “concert” meant an agreement. In 1744 Scottish ministers invited believers to pray at the same set times for the spread of the gospel, and in 1747 Jonathan Edwards urged Americans to join them in A Humble Attempt (Volume 7, chapter 9). In 1784 English Baptists read Edwards’s book and set apart the first Monday evening of every month for prayer (Volume 7, chapter 16).

  1. Find believers, near or far, who will pray with you.
  2. Agree on a time, such as the first Monday of each month.
  3. Agree on what to ask: the spread of the gospel, revival, one country.
  4. At that time, pray wherever you are, alone or together.

A sick person or a believer in a hostile land can join without leaving home.

ACTS

ACTS is a modern teaching aid, not a method of the old witnesses. Its letters stand for Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication (asking). But each part is old. Müller found his Bible reading led him “to confession, or to thanksgiving, or to intercession, or to supplication” (Volume 8, chapter 5), and Paul urged “requests, prayers, intercessions and thanks” for everyone (1 Timothy 2:1).

  1. Adoration. Praise God for who He is: holy, faithful, loving, all-powerful.
  2. Confession. Tell Him your sins honestly, and trust His forgiveness in Christ.
  3. Thanksgiving. Thank Him for specific gifts.
  4. Supplication. Ask for your needs and the needs of others.

It is a help, not a law: some days you will begin with your tears.

Praying by name

At Mukti in India, Pandita Ramabai’s household prayed for more than twenty-nine thousand people by name (Volume 9, chapter 2). Lancelot Andrewes kept a notebook of prayers for each day of the week, with lists of people to pray for (Volume 6, chapter 11).

  1. Write down names: family, friends, neighbors, church leaders, people who do not yet know Christ.
  2. Spread them over the days of the week, a few names for each day.
  3. You can write each name on a small card, with one or two needs.
  4. Pray for each person by name, with one clear request.
  5. Note answers when they come, and add names as God brings them to mind.

If you cannot write, choose seven people and remember one on each day of the week.

Prayer walking

Prayer walking means praying for a place as you walk through it. God told His exiles, “Seek the peace of the city ... and pray to the LORD for it” (Jeremiah 29:7). Believers in Argentina prayed for their cities street by street, and teams walked quietly through distant cities during the 10/40 Window prayer movement (Volume 10, chapters 13 and 14). Charles Finney once urged believers in Bolton to go two by two and pray in every house that would let them (Volume 10, chapter 14).

  1. Choose a route: your street, the road to work, the area around your church.
  2. Walk slowly, praying silently or quietly, eyes open.
  3. As you pass each home or shop, pray, “Peace be on this household” (Luke 10:5).
  4. If a neighbor greets you, you may ask, “How can I pray for you?”

Pray to bless, not to be seen. Where Christians are a watched minority, pray silently and draw no attention.

Fasting with prayer

Fasting means going without food, or something else, for a time, to give that time to God. Nehemiah fasted and prayed when he heard the news from Jerusalem (Volume 1, chapter 15). In Volume 3, chapter 9, the church at Antioch was “serving the Lord in worship and fasting” when the Spirit sent out Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:2). The Didache set Wednesdays and Fridays as fast days (Volume 4, chapter 1), and in our own time Bill Bright and Derek Prince called many to fast (Volume 10, chapter 10). Chapter 4 of this book, “Prayer and Fasting,” gathers what the witnesses teach.

  1. Begin small: skip one meal and give that time to prayer.
  2. Keep it quiet, “so that no one but your Father, who is there in secret, will know” (Matthew 6:18).
  3. Let each hunger pang remind you of your request.
  4. Share what you saved with the hungry, as Isaiah 58 teaches.

Health first. Some should not go without food at all: pregnant or nursing mothers, children, people with diabetes, heart or kidney disease, people who have struggled with eating disorders, and people on certain medicines. If you are not sure, ask a doctor or health worker. You can fast from something else instead, such as your phone or a favorite food.

Praying through the night

Jesus “stayed up all night in prayer to God” before choosing His apostles (Luke 6:12). The psalmist wrote, “In the middle of the night I get up to thank You” (Psalm 119:62), and Lancelot Andrewes counted midnight among the times of prayer (Volume 6, chapter 11). The Moravians at Herrnhut kept a watch of prayer one hour at a time, day and night (Volume 7, chapter 4), and believers across Africa gather for all-night vigils (Volume 10, chapter 17).

  1. Do not begin with a whole night alone. Join others, or take one hour, as the Moravians did.
  2. Plan the time: songs, Scripture, confession, thanks and a list of needs.
  3. Change your posture: sit, stand, kneel, walk. Take short breaks.
  4. If you wake in the night, pray for a few minutes instead of worrying (Psalm 63:6).

With care. A vigil does not earn God’s answer, and those who cannot come are not second-class believers. God “gives sleep to the one He loves” (Psalm 127:2). The sick, the old, parents of small children and those with heavy work next day should guard their rest.

A family prayer time

Moses told parents to speak of God’s words “as you sit in your house and as you go on your way, as you lie down and as you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Macrina made her family home a house of prayer (Volume 4, chapter 12), and Susanna Wesley, in a crowded house, kept her times with God and gave each child an evening alone with her (Volume 7, chapter 6). Chapter 10 of this book, “The Family Altar,” says more.

  1. Choose a time that suits your home, such as after the evening meal.
  2. Keep it short: ten minutes, and less for small children.
  3. Read a few verses or a Bible story, and welcome the children’s questions.
  4. Let each person name one thing to thank God for and one thing to ask.
  5. Let everyone pray, even the youngest. End with the Lord’s Prayer or a song.

If you are the only believer at home, pray for your family by name.

Praying for the persecuted church

“Keep in mind those in prison, as if you were in chains alongside them” (Hebrews 13:3). In Volume 3, chapter 8, while Peter was in prison, “the church was praying to God for him without letup” (Acts 12:5). In our own time we met Helen Berhane in her shipping container in Eritrea (Volume 10, chapter 18), the house churches of China (Volume 10, chapter 9) and Iran (Volume 10, chapter 19), and Brother Andrew, who carried Bibles across closed borders (Volume 10, chapter 3).

  1. Choose one country where Christians suffer for their faith, and pray for its believers daily.
  2. Pray for their needs: food, health and safety for prisoners and their families.
  3. Pray for their faith: courage, joy and the comfort of the Scriptures.
  4. Pray for those who persecute them, as Clement prayed for the rulers of Rome (Volume 4, chapter 2).

Protect those you pray for. Never share the names, places or meeting details of believers in danger, even in a prayer request or online.
